segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The farmhouse stood a quarter of a mile back along the road, and its mistress let them the kitchen for a shilling and their supper for another, having first satisfied herself that they were not married and then, being a practical woman, deciding she did not much care either way. The driver ate his bacon standing and walked on to Itchen Vale, meaning to be at the wheelwright's door by daylight. That left the fire, two settles, and the farmer's wife in the corner with a heap of mending she intended to finish and was asleep over within the half hour.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Judith laid the dispensing book flat on the settle beside her, as promised.

segments.speaker: Miss Judith Vane
segments.text: You have never once said where you were.

segments.speaker: Captain Nathaniel Farr
segments.text: You have never once asked.

segments.speaker: Miss Judith Vane
segments.text: I am asking now, and there is nowhere for either of us to go until morning, so you may as well be thorough.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He took his time about it, and when it came it came in the flattest voice she had ever heard used upon such matters.

segments.speaker: Captain Nathaniel Farr
segments.text: There was a ford. I could not tell you its name; I never learnt it. My horse went down in it and I went down under the horse, and what I chiefly remember is being angry about the horse. They carried me off to a house at Lisbon that had been a convent and was then whatever they wanted it to be. I was thirteen months in it. Nine of those I could not have told you what county I was born in.

segments.speaker: Miss Judith Vane
segments.text: Thirteen months.

segments.speaker: Captain Nathaniel Farr
segments.text: The regiment did not wait. They went up into France in the spring and my name stayed behind on a list of men not answered for, and some clerk with a great deal to do drew a line through it. I do not blame the clerk. I have been that clerk.

segments.speaker: Miss Judith Vane
segments.text: And you wrote.

segments.speaker: Captain Nathaniel Farr
segments.text: Twice, when I could hold a pen. To my great-uncle, both of them, and gave them to a commissary going home who swore he would see them to the packet. Nothing came back. Nothing was ever going to come back, because anything sent to me went after the regiment, and the regiment had no fixed direction from one month to the next. A letter to a man in a hospital is a letter to nobody in particular.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The fire dropped. Judith put her hands together in her lap and looked at them, which for her was very nearly hiding.

segments.speaker: Miss Judith Vane
segments.text: We had it here in the November of the year thirteen. Mrs Pike brought it up to the library with the rest of the news, and I said how very shocking, and asked whether the coach had come, and went home and finished the ironing.

segments.speaker: Captain Nathaniel Farr
segments.text: That is what one says.

segments.speaker: Miss Judith Vane
segments.text: It is. I also took the third volume of Anson out of the library that same week and kept it eleven months and paid the fine myself and told Owen I had mislaid it. I had not mislaid it. It was under my bed. I could not have worn black for you, Captain. I had no right to it and the parish would have wanted to know on what grounds. So I kept your book instead, and that was the whole of it, and now you know a thing about me that nobody else does.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He did not answer that at all, which she found she preferred to any of the things he might have said.

segments.speaker: Captain Nathaniel Farr
segments.text: April. She wrote in April.

segments.speaker: Miss Judith Vane
segments.text: April, at lambing. And Mr Hartwell had taken charge of the post in March. A letter out of Oakmere does not walk to Winchester by itself. It goes down the lane to the Bell for the Tuesday or the Friday coach, and it must be carried by somebody, and paid for by somebody, and that somebody had been him for six weeks already.

segments.speaker: Captain Nathaniel Farr
segments.text: He never saw her write it. She burnt two by her own account and took three nights over it.

segments.speaker: Miss Judith Vane
segments.text: He did not need to see her write it. She put it into his hand at her own kitchen table and told him what it was. She would have told him. She is not a woman who hands over a thing without explaining it.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Farr turned that over. The arithmetic was not difficult, and that was rather the worst of it.

segments.speaker: Captain Nathaniel Farr
segments.text: If that letter had gone, and if it had found me, I should have been at Oakmere by August. My great-uncle would have had me at his own fire in August, and no clerk from Winchester would have come out with a paper in September, because there would have been nothing left to draw one about.

segments.speaker: Miss Judith Vane
segments.text: One man in England lost everything by that letter arriving. He was holding it.

segments.speaker: Captain Nathaniel Farr
segments.text: Then he burnt it in the parlour grate and I shall never prove a word of it.

segments.speaker: Miss Judith Vane
segments.text: Perhaps. But a man who burns a letter must first decide to be that sort of man, and Mr Hartwell strikes me as one who would very much rather not decide anything so plainly. It is far easier to carry a letter to the Bell with a direction on it that will never answer, and let the post do the burning for you. And the post does not burn things, Captain. It keeps them. Somewhere in this county there is a shelf with that letter on it, and I mean to ask Mr Cobbold in the morning where such a shelf would be.
